newsitem.title: UK: Price drop ambushes UK wheat farmers.
newsitem.headline: Price drop ambushes UK wheat farmers.

text.p: Soaring grain prices of a few months ago tempted British farmers to sow more land to winter wheat for next year only to see them buckle under the bumper 1996 harvest that has just been gathered.

Seed merchants said most land freed from the European Union's (EU) set-aside scheme had been used for wheat this year and very little had gone to barley. Winter linseed plantings had also increased sharply.
But just a month after new seeds were drilled in, farmers worry about their crop decisions.

"There is a lot more wheat this year as prices looked a lot better. But it may not be the right thing to do," said Bernard Martin, crop analyst for consultancy firm ADAS in East Anglia -- the UK top cereal growing region.
Generous supply is entering a falling market and traders reckon exports may not match surplus availability this year unless prices ease further.
The Ministry of Agriculture (MAFF) estimated the 1996 wheat crop sharply higher at 15.9 million tonnes from 14.3 million last year, while barley was up to 7.9 million from 6.8 million.
"We've got a bumper harvest, but nowhere to export it to because the (European) Commission doesn't want to rock the boat with the U.S. by granting decent restitution," said one trader in London.
The Commission has to juggle a tight budget to provide aid to distressed beef farmers because of the Mad Cow crisis yet respond to pressure to move surplus grain swiftly to exports.

On the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE), the benchmark November wheat contract has seen new lows almost every day since the beginning of September, shedding 20 percent since the peak in April.
Traders reckon about half of that fall to 97.50 stg on Tuesday was due to sterling's strength.
But Steve Thornhill, head of economics and research at the Home-Grown Cereals Authority (HGCA), said prices would need to remain competitively low to get a decent flow of export business.
"What we don't want to happen is for supplies not to move to the market. We want to keep them moving," Thornhill said.
The HGCA forecast surplus wheat availability at a hefty 4.5-5 million tonnes this season from 3.2 million tonnes in 1995/96.

ADAS's Martin said he had recommended farmers to rest the wheat soil for a year and rotate to peas and beans. But his advice went mostly ignored at a time when a price uptrend looked a valid argument.
"There is an increase in second wheats this year," he said.

Crop experts said about two thirds of the five percentage point cut in set-side was planted to wheat and about one third to barley. Milling wheat sowings increased, but not to the extent of recovering from a decline over the last few years. Malting barley plantings received a knock this year after relatively poor quality last season, farm advisors said.
